item.title: Green-card holders say ICE is using decades-old minor infractions to detain them
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
In the three decades that San Juanita Guerra had been crossing into Mexico to fill prescriptions, she never had a problem returning home to the United States. But last March, officers at a South Texas port of entry detained the then-74-year-old green-card holder. Border officials had taken her fingerprints and discovered a 30-year-old conviction on a weapons charge. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Guerra had no criminal record in the years since, and the misdemeanor had not prevented her from renewing her status three times. Nor had it come up during the hundreds of trips she had taken to Mexico, said her attorney, Wendoli Rodriguez. But now legal permanent residents - immigrants granted the right to live and work indefinitely in the United States - are finding that their status is not as secure as many previously thought. Attorneys say clients are getting flagged at border crossings and airports by officers who are checking identification cards and flight manifests. In some cases, authorities are detaining people over decades-old charges that did not come up when they applied for or renewed their green cards and that in the past would have resulted in a citation - not an effort to remove legal status. The detentions mark a shift in how President Donald Trump’s administration is treating a group of immigrants who already have undergone vetting and in many cases have lived for extended periods in the United States. Some immigrants, like Guerra, are being accused of not disclosing the charges when they submitted that paperwork. Attorneys and relatives for several recently detained longtime permanent residents said in some cases charges had been expunged or dismissed. They say the omission was a mistake, not an attempt to commit fraud. “I tell all my clients, if you have a green card, just stay home. Don’t travel, it’s not a good time for that,” said Jodi Goodwin, an immigration attorney in Texas. “They will use anything to try to detain someone.” One green-card holder, Emiliano Andrade Covarrubias, died in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody last month after he was stopped at a port of entry while returning to the United States from Mexico. The Department of Homeland Security accused the 56-year-old of obtaining his green card without telling U.S. Customs and Immigration Services that he had faced theft charges years earlier. States cooperating with DHS, such as Florida and Texas, have granted the agency access to a wealth of information about its residents, handing over databases with information on criminal records, voter registrations and more. Officers use powerful surveillance, digital forensics and data-mining tools employing artificial intelligence to pinpoint information that could lead to an arrest or termination of a permanent status. Federal agencies such as the Transportation Security Administration also are sharing information with DHS that permits officers to identify violations that could lead to a green card being revoked - such as tax evasion or staying outside the United States for more than six months. DHS did not respond to a request for comment on how many green-card holders it has detained. The agency has argued that reviews are essential for safeguarding the country and that no noncitizen should ever feel their stay in the United States is unconditional. Port officials in Texas said they always have conducted these checks and denied following any specific directives or arrest quotas from the Trump administration. The information that officers are using to detain people can offer an incomplete picture of what transpired in someone’s past, several attorneys said. John Gihon, a former ICE attorney who now practices immigration law in Florida, described the example of one client who has been a permanent resident for decades and accidentally registered to vote after receiving the forms in the mail. While traveling back to the United States recently, ICE detained him at the airport. In court, Gihon demonstrated that his client had not falsely claimed to be a citizen on the voter-registration forms. The local supervisor of elections wrote a letter apologizing for mistakenly processing the registration. Gihon did not name the client, saying he wanted to protect the man’s identity. “It wasn’t the crime of the century,” Gihon said. “We won his case, and he kept his green card. But he didn’t deserve to sleep on a pee-stained mattress in detention for weeks. That’s unnecessary.” Lawful permanent residents must disclose any criminal history when seeking a green card, even if the charge ultimately was dismissed, in addition to other information such as financial records. Attorneys and advocates said many lawful permanent residents successfully challenge their detentions in immigration court and keep their green cards. But being held for weeks or months is nonetheless challenging for both the individual and their family. Andrade Covarrubias, the man found dead at a South Texas detention center in October, spent months fighting his case as his health deteriorated. The longtime Dallas resident obtained a green card in 2019, and ran a contracting and painting business with his son. He had been charged with theft in 2004. His daughter Estefani Andrade said he had taken a ladder after a client failed to pay him. Monica Yoas, an ICE spokeswoman, said in a statement that Andrade Covarrubias was attempting to enter Laredo, Texas, on June 26 when agents determined he had “obtained status through fraudulent means by failing to disclose his previous arrest during the review process.” She added that “He was receiving due process.” Dallas County records show the father of three pleaded no contest to the misdemeanor charge. He received deferred adjudication from the judge - meaning it did not appear as a conviction on his record. Andrade Covarrubias served probation and had the option of having the charge expunged. Texas border attorney Jaime Diez said he has handled at least 100 cases in the last 18 months in which green-card holders were detained. In several, he said, officers acted on information that proved incorrect. He described the case of a 65-year-old woman who had gone to Mexico for a church retreat. When she returned, officers questioned whether she had registered to vote in 1995. The woman, whom Diez declined to name, has had a green card since 1987. She was detained for 10 days, and the case against her was dismissed because officers were unable to prove that she had indeed registered. “They are focusing on finding things to make you ineligible to stay here,” he said. “And they are doing it without any consequences.” Andrade Covarrubias, who ICE said had been receiving proper care and had a “documented medical history of diabetes, hypertension, and anxiety,” was found unresponsive Oct. 17 in his detention bed. He was pronounced dead moments later. Andrade said it was clear from her father’s deterioration that he was not receiving adequate care or his medications regularly while detained. “We have always felt that the circumstances surrounding his case and the way he was treated deserved to be heard,” said Andrade, who helped her father complete the green-card paperwork and process as a teenager. “We don’t want what happened to him to be forgotten.” In Guerra’s case, the September 1994 weapons charge stemmed from a family crisis and a mistake, said her daughter Carla Gomez. One of Guerra’s teenage children had been struggling with suicidal thoughts and obtained a gun. The single mother took the gun and put it in her purse, Guerra said in an interview. Two days later, Guerra went to pick up her sister at McAllen International Airport in Texas’s Rio Grande Valley. While there, airport security detected the unloaded pistol and charged her with unlawfully carrying a weapon, according to Hidalgo County court records. Guerra said her attorney at the time advised her to plead guilty to the misdemeanor charge. She paid a fine and was briefly on probation. Then the case was dismissed. Guerra, now 75, obtained her green card a decade before the incident with the firearm. Authorities did not terminate her status as a result of the charge, and Guerra said she mistakenly thought it had been wiped from her record. A notary public erroneously advised her that she didn’t need to disclose it on future applications, she added. But on March 2, officials at the Progreso port of entry - a popular crossing for medical tourists and day shoppers - took Guerra’s fingerprints after she forgot her green card at home. One of her daughters brought the documents to the port office. They expected the matter to clear up. But the biometric database pinged Guerra’s 30-year-old conviction. “Yo cumplí con todo. … Se lo expliqué,” Guerra recalled telling the officer. “I’m done with that. … I explained what happened.” ICE officers shackled her. She spent 22 days in detention, where relatives say she didn’t sleep or eat well. Guerra said younger detainees took pity on her and found extra mats to give the older woman more cushion for her ailing hip. But nothing helped. She became severely disoriented and weak. Gomez, her daughter, said fellow detainees contacted her, saying that if she didn’t get Guerra out soon, the woman would die there. The family rallied community support, an attorney immediately filed for a bond hearing, and an immigration judge granted the request. “I had to move quickly because she was declining rapidly in detention,” said Rodriguez, her attorney. Guerra was outfitted with an ankle bracelet to track her whereabouts, though it was later removed after she raised health concerns. Her family is still trying to pay back the $15,000 they borrowed to secure her release. She has a hearing scheduled for later this month. Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/immigration/2026/11/17/they-had-green-cards-years-then-they-were-detained-by-ice/

item.title: Democrats see an immigration opening despite Stephen Miller's rise
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
In the days before the midterm election, Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) felt confident that a blue wave could open the door to immigration reform. Cuellar was so bullish that he reached out to acting Immigration and Customs Enforcement director David Venturella and the Customs and Border Protection commissioner Rodney Scott to feel out areas of “common ground,” he said in an interview. Now Cuellar is one of several moderate Democrats angling to strike a deal with the White House, especially on reining in ICE officers and creating legal pathways to citizenship for some immigrants. They’re undeterred by President Donald Trump’s elevation of immigration hardliner Stephen Miller to chief of staff. And they’re buoyed by Trump’s recent admission that his deportations policy was “too tough.” Several of these Democrats have already placed calls to Trump and DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin to express a willingness to work together. Cuellar said he reached back out to Venturella and Scott after the election to try to schedule meetings. “If the president, as the president of the United States, makes a decision — and not a chief of staff — we can get the job done,” Cuellar said in an interview. “I’m sure we’re going to find a lot of differences, but if we sit down, we can definitely resolve them.” It’ll be a tough road: Securing buy-in from the White House becomes undoubtedly more complicated with Miller, a champion of the administration’s aggressive deportation push. Republicans in Congress have largely been willing to defer to the president on the issue. And Democratic leaders have questioned Trump’s sincerity and said they have no interest in working with Miller. The possibility will become even more tenuous once Democrats begin investigating the Trump administration, including the president’s immigration enforcement agencies. CBP and ICE did not respond to requests for comment. Neither did Democratic leaders Sen. Chuck Schumer and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries. Democrats like Cuellar, Sen.-elects James Talarico of Texas and Annie Andrews of South Carolina are aware of all of those hurdles. But they’re betting the midterms have created an opening for serious talks: Latino voters across the country swung hard back toward Democrats this cycle, and more and more Republicans are recognizing that their immigration agenda hurt them politically. Talarico and Andrews have publicly expressed interest in working with the president on immigration, and both ran on platforms that emphasized creating paths to citizenship for undocumented immigrants. “I’m ready to work with President Trump to fix this broken immigration system,” Talarico said in a statement. Inside the White House, there’s a recognition that the president will proceed however he so chooses, regardless of who the chief of staff is. Trump is accessible to outside voices — journalists, business leaders and lawmakers regularly call him directly — and often poses policy questions to aides and allies as he decides which direction he will go. “Everybody’s like, ‘Well, it’s never going to happen with Stephen Miller.’ Look, Donald Trump’s the president. I don’t care if Stephen Miller’s the chief of staff or Susie Wiles or John Kelly or whoever the chief of staff might be,” said a person close to the White House, granted anonymity to speak about the internal dynamic. For Democrats, there’s a real political incentive to getting a deal done ahead of a critical 2028 presidential election — especially as the party seeks to win back voter trust on immigration and border security, policy areas that spelled doom for them in 2024. “You have these Democrats who flip red states, and it’s also to their self-interest, right? Not just to do rhetoric, and go big or go home, but actually come to the middle with the president, with the Republicans. Because if not, I think that the big lesson this election is, Hispanic voters are gonna flip back ... if they don’t see Democrats delivering anything the next two years,” said Rebecca Shi, the executive director of ABIC, a coalition of pro-immigration reform business executives. She added that there’s a lesson for Republicans, too, if they don’t come to the table: “They will lose the White House.” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis touted Trump’s immigration accomplishments, including border security, a drop in crime and the creation of the Homeland Security Task Force and said the president’s “strong immigration policy remains unchanged.” She said Democrats should work alongside Trump to “keep our southern border secure, remove dangerous illegal criminals from our communities, and stop the illicit trafficking of lethal drugs.” Democrats welcomed the president’s remarks on 60 Minutes on Sunday, when he said he was open to legal pathways for some unauthorized immigrants who haven’t committed crimes and are working and contributing to the economy. Mullin also floated an openness to a bipartisan immigration overhaul involving DACA, which could provide permanent legal status to some undocumented immigrants who arrived in the U.S. as children, even as he — and the president — have insisted that any proposal wouldn’t include amnesty. In a sign that Democrats have learned the lessons of the Biden administration , many of them are eager to pair reforms with border security measures. Cuellar, who will chair the Homeland Security Appropriations subcommittee in the next conference, has long suggested including guardrails on ICE in the next funding bill, such as requiring judicial warrants, rolling out body camera usage and restoring “sensitive locations” such as churches and schools as off-limits. Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), another Democrat who has expressed interest in working with the Trump administration, said that beyond “talk,” it would help to see some smaller concrete policy shifts from the White House to affirm that Trump is, in fact, open to changes to the immigration system. “The way to do that is to have some reforms already at ICE — whether it’s shutting down these detention centers, giving certain level of protections, whether to veterans, so they don't get deported, to maybe parents of U.S. citizens, they don’t get deported — something to show that, you know, it's not just talk, this isn’t going to be a policy led by Stephen Miller,” he said. But Miller remains a bogeyman for Democrats, someone they view as responsible for the president’s most extreme immigration policies. As chief of staff, he can ensure he’s one of the last people in the president’s ear — and that the White House doesn’t bend to what he sees as unrealistic Democratic demands. “The reason why they wouldn’t do an amnesty deal, I believe, is because it would be the ultimate and most public contradiction of the central thesis of this entire political program as it was sold to voters,” said Mike Howell, president of the Oversight Project and a member of the Mass Deportation Coalition. “It would be the end of the America First coalition as it currently exists.” Democrats' distrust of Miller will also make it challenging for them to align on any potential deal with the White House. “Stephen Miller is the mastermind and architect of terror, and death, and illegality in this country, and he is not anyone who even understands truthfully what immigration policy should look like,” said Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif). “No deals, man. No deals,” she added. The White House pointed to Miller’s experience on the Hill as a valuable asset. White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said unlike Democrats “who refused to work with the President and blocked many of his popular policies, Stephen Miller has a track record of spearheading bipartisan efforts: public safety reform, making our cities such as Washington, D.C. and Memphis safe again, drug pricing transparency, and unleashing a nuclear energy renaissance.” Lawmakers are waiting for the president to make the first move. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who will continue to lead his fellow Republicans when Democrats retake control of the Senate this January, told reporters after the election that “if there's something he wants to do there, we can have that conversation.” “There are always some landmines, which is why in the past the wheels have kind of come off, despite some really good efforts at trying to find a landing spot. But yeah we're open to something he wants to propose,” Thune added. Jordain Carney contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/17/democrats-trump-immigration-reform-01168941

item.title: Ukraine strikes key Russian supply route just days before Trump-Putin talks
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridge Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making. Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort. The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack. Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - had been closed after Russia hit Ukraine's capital overnight. The Southern bridge partially reopened on Tuesday, Klitschko said. Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good. While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin. The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight. The Crimean Bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014. The $3.6bn (£2.7bn) piece of infrastructure is widely seen in Russia and Ukraine as Putin's personal pet project: His close tycoon friend Arkady Rotenberg built it, and then Putin personally opened it by driving a lorry over it in May 2018. Putin (centre) personally opened the Crimean Bridge by driving a lorry over it in May 2018 [Anadolu Agency/Getty Images] In Ukraine, the much-hated bridge is seen as one of the main symbols of Russia's continuing occupation of Ukrainian lands. "We're drinking champagne!" Andrii, an engineer who lives in Kyiv, told the BBC. He said the latest attack would "deal a very heavy blow to the morale of the Russians". Some Ukrainians are concerned that Putin might now respond by carrying out even more attacks against civilian infrastructure, but Andrii said: "I don't think the Russians can make things much worse; they're already pounding us every single night with everything they've got." Images show the damage to the Crimean Bridge from the overnight attack [BBC] The damage after the overnight attack, involving cruise missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section apparently destroyed. Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below. Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective". He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage". The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and Russia's transport ministry later said some rail services resumed. Ukraine's state security service SBU said its operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders". Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch. [BBC] Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China. Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations". For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry. Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday. In Kyiv, loud explosions were heard just before midnight on Monday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies. On Tuesday, Zelensky said four ballistic missiles had targeted the Southern Bridge, and another three had been fired on the Northern Bridge. Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were also damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters. Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River, connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city. Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials. [BBC] The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear, though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly. The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired. However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar. This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo. There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack. Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area. In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel. This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdyansk. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control. item.title: Trump responds to Iran ‘dirty bomb’ report as White House says ‘no credible threats’
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump has said Iran will “pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before” if there is any threat to Washington D.C., after U.S. intelligence found Iran could be developing plans to detonate a so-called dirty bomb or chemical weapon in the nation’s capital. Speaking in Manilla on Tuesday, Trump said: “Well, if there is… they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before. I hope it’s not, but we take it very seriously, because they happen to be crazy. This is why they can’t have a nuclear weapon by the way.” The White House told Newsweek there were currently “no credible threats” after a CNN report citing seven U.S. officials stated that new intelligence pointed to a potential effort to target senior Trump administration officials. “We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement to Newsweek on Monday. Sources familiar with the intelligence characterized the planning as an effort to give Iran options, rather than an indication of an imminent attack. The report said officials remained divided over the credibility of the intelligence and whether Iran had the personnel in place to carry out such a plot. Newsweek reached out to Iran’s Mission to the United Nations for comment. A spokesperson for the mission told CNN that Tehran considers the use of chemical weapons under any circumstances to be “wholly illegitimate and categorically rejects and unequivocally refutes the false and fabricated allegations circulated in this regard.” Esmaeil Baqaei, a spokesman for Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, called the reports of the dirty bomb plot “baseless allegations.” What Is A Dirty Bomb? A dirty bomb is a conventional explosive device combined with radioactive material. The blast from such a device spreads dust, fragments and radioactive material into the surrounding area, which could leave its victims exposed to radiation through inhalation, ingestion, or direct contact. It differs from a nuclear bomb because a regular explosive is used rather than creating a nuclear chain reaction. A dirty bomb could impact several city blocks, whereas a nuclear blast would vaporize much of a city. A dirty bomb is easier to construct than a nuclear weapon because it does not require a sustained nuclear chain reaction or weapons-grade design. However, sufficient radioactive material would have to be obtained and delivered for it to be effective. Why It Matters The reported intelligence comes amid broader concerns of Iranian threats against senior U.S. officials. Newsweek reported last week that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had moved out of his Washington-area home and onto a military base following threats against his life from Iran. Bessent’s relocation came as U.S. officials assessed that Iranian efforts to target current and former American officials had reached a more advanced stage. He was the third Trump Cabinet member reported to have moved into military housing, following Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Reports have since indicated that Attorney General Todd Blanche has also been living at a military installation in the Washington D.C. area for months. While speaking to reporters outside the White House on Monday, Trump was asked whether he was concerned about being targeted by Iranian drones. “I’m worried about you, because if they get me, you’re gone too. Be careful,” Trump said. The president has sent mixed signals about the next steps in the war, at times threatening further military action against Iran while saying the conflict is “militarily…effectively over.” Last week, he warned that U.S. forces were “locked and loaded,” and said Washington was monitoring Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran’s nuclear program, for signs of activity. Q: Are you worried about Iranian drones targeting you? TRUMP: I'm worried about you, because if they get me, you're gone too. Be careful. pic.twitter.com/EWp6AOQs0K — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) November 16, 2026 CNN senior national security reporter Katie Bo Lillis said U.S. officials were reportedly taking the new intel “very, very seriously.” “It sparked a real flurry of kind of planning efforts, of contingency planning efforts, here in Washington,” Lillis said Monday on the network. Meanwhile, the U.S. is continuing to bolster its military presence in the Middle East as Trump weighs his next steps in the conflict. A third American aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt , arrived in the region on Monday , U.S. Central Command said in a social media post. The carrier adds to the already substantial U.S. military buildup near Iran, joining the thousands of troops already deployed aboard the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington . USS Theodore Roosevelt is seen leaving the Navy port of Yokosuka, near Tokyo, on October 19. The Strait of Hormuz remains a major flashpoint in the conflict, with commercial shipping continuing to face attacks and other risks. The waterway, through which roughly a fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war, has seen traffic fall to less than a third of prewar levels, according to independent maritime assessments. Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps navy said mines had damaged six oil tankers since Sunday. The conflict has also contributed to higher costs for Americans, particularly at the gas pump, as disruptions to global oil supplies have pushed up energy prices. Gas prices have since eased, falling below $4 per gallon for the first time since July, AAA reported Friday, but remain nearly a dollar higher than a year ago. The national average stood at $3.81 per gallon on Monday. “These trends may continue, as the International Energy Agency has raised its oil production forecast, putting additional pressure on oil prices as shipments ramp up through the Strait of Hormuz,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a statement Monday. “GasBuddy expects the national average price of gasoline to fall this week to its lowest level since March, dropping below $3.72 per gallon.” Vice President JD Vance defended the administration’s handling of the Iran war in an interview with Fox News host Laura Ingraham on Monday. Vance said Trump could either end the military campaign or apply further military and diplomatic pressure on Iran, but insisted the president would not allow the conflict to become a prolonged commitment. “We are not going to allow this to become a 10- or 15-year commitment, or, frankly, even a two-year commitment, despite the fact that a lot of neoconservatives and a lot of other people want us to stay there forever,” Vance said. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here . Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Steven Frank , Edward T. Cummins and Emma Lee-Sang Update 11/17/26, 7 a.m. ET: This article was updated with additional information. item.title: Trump signs trade 'statement' with Thailand, says deal will be finalized in 'coming weeks'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump is traveling to Asia for meetings with global leaders and for his second visit to China for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. See the most recent developments below. Latest Developments Nov 17, 8:22 AM Trump signs trade 'statement' with Thailand, says deal will be finalized in 'coming weeks' President Donald Trump and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul signed a joint trade statement on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit in Manila, the Philippines, on Tuesday, saying the formal agreement will be finalized "in the coming weeks." "It's a joint statement agreement between United States of America, the Kingdom of Thailand, on reciprocal trade. It's a very big, actually, it's a very big trade deal," Trump said, after he was asked about the document he signed, given that a formal trade deal has not yet been reached. Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: Thailand's Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and President Donald Trump in Manila on Nov. 17, 2026. "And I look forward to finalizing the details of our formal agreement in the coming weeks," Trump said earlier. "Our staff is working on it very diligently, and it'll be done. But the concept of what we have will be really very permanent, and we're just about there." The Thai prime minister also pointed out that there is "still more" work to do, but said he is confident an agreement would be reached "soon." "I believe the agreement will bring greater dynamics to our trade relations and open new opportunities for all stakeholders," Charnvirakul said. "Mr. President, your leadership in bringing this negotiation to a nice conclusion like this is greatly appreciated. Yet there is still a little more to do. I'm confident that the agreement will be ready for us to sign real soon." Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: Thailand's Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and US President Donald Trump shake hands in Manila on Nov. 17, 2026. According to Trump, Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on U.S. exports under the deal, in addition to removing "substantial non-tariff barriers on American vehicles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol, and poultry" and purchasing $2.6 billion in U.S. agricultural products. item.title: Duffy wants $50 billion to avert ground stops. Experts say money isn't the issue.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Just two months ago, the nation's top aviation official sounded pretty pleased with Congress and its financial support for modernizing the nation's air traffic systems. "That initial $12.5 billion investment?" FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said during a House hearing, sounding bullish on the agency's progress. "Yes, it's allowing us to build a solid foundation." Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. But that $12.5 billion emerged as a contentious flashpoint after Friday's calamitous 4½-hour nationwide ground stop trigged by a telecommunications failure. In the days since, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, with Bedford often by his side, has repeatedly complained about what he says is a lack of money for the FAA to update its systems, implying that Friday's stoppage could've been avoided if only the agency had received more funding. Duffy, turning the outage into a fundraising appeal, made his case again Monday. The FAA needed billions more for the contractors to begin work on the next stage of updating systems, he said. "They're ready to go and work with us at a very fast pace. I just can't tell them to go until we get the money for investment," Duffy said about the project's contractors in a CNBC clip he reposted on social media. But the surprise ground stop was not tied to a lack of funding, according to experts and former agency officials. "That's not what caused Friday," said Tom Lintner, a former FAA air traffic program manager. "Four decades of procrastination and poor program management is what caused Friday." Outside experts say transitioning from old systems needs to be done with more extensive planning and care, with backup plans for backup plans, so that a single point of vulnerability - in this case an overactive router in Arkansas - doesn't bring the nation's aviation industry to a halt. Congress gave the FAA $12.5 billion last year as down payment on its efforts, such as replacing old copper wire with new fiber cables - the same work that is believed to have caused the technical issues that resulted in Friday's decision to close down the airspace. Duffy acknowledged that first installment of money, but he said the FAA now needed $30.1 billion more for a more extensive modernization effort. On Friday night, he upped the request to $50 billion. He acknowledged the fluctuating figures. "I was trying to get a number that I think Congress will give me," he said Saturday. But the proposed $30 billion funding package - or $50 billion - is only partly aimed at air traffic modernization. About $10 billion is for a long-range plan to update the air traffic controller computer platform and workstations. Another $10 billion is for renovating air traffic control towers and grants to improve airport runways and terminals. Another $10 billion is to replace or renovate certain airport terminals. So most of the $50 billion ask has little to do with improving safety, said Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) said on his podcast Monday. "In a time where we've got massive national debt, I'm not sure expanding amenities at airports is a critical priority," Cruz said, "but safety most definitely is a critical priority." The FAA's initial modernization push received bipartisan support. At the House hearing in September, Bedford thanked President Donald Trump, Duffy and Congress for passing "a historic $12.5 billion down-payment," noting that, "We are executing on the most ambitious modernization project of our time and delivering it in record time." Now, as the ask has escalated, some Democrats on Capitol Hill have objected that the original $12.5 billion hasn't even been fully exhausted. The FAA so far has spent only about $1 billion of the funding it requested, with another $4.3 billion obligated to projects, said Reps. Rick Larsen of Washington and Andre Carson of Indiana. The ground stop was an expensive interruption for major U.S. airlines, according to report from the brokerage firm Bernstein. Bernstein analysts estimated the stoppage cost American, Delta, United and Southwest about $345 million. A main driver was the thousands of canceled flights and refunds for passengers who decided not to rebook their flights. item.title: Disney says it needs to cut $3 billion in costs: 'Changes like these are not easy’
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Disney's ( DIS ) fourth quarter earnings beat expectations as the media giant's parks and streaming businesses continued to deliver strong growth while the company focused on streamlining operations. The stock rose 2% in early trading as investors homed in on plans to cut costs by roughly $3 billion by 2029. "Most of the savings will be used to fund future growth," new CEO Josh D'Amaro told investors on the earnings call. "Now, changes like these are not easy, and they affect people … these steps are important if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment, and keeps investing in the content and technology that will drive our growth." Disney's cost-cutting efforts follow the company's late-September job cuts of approximately 300 roles across human resources and tech. The company said it is using artificial intelligence to accelerate pre- and postproduction processes, design planning around experiences, and operations. In fiscal Q4, Disney posted adjusted earnings per share of $1.77, above the $1.68 Wall Street expected, alongside revenue of $25.9 billion, which was slightly above the $25.2 billion forecast, according to Bloomberg consensus data. "Our strong fiscal 2026 results, delivered amid a challenging macroeconomic environment, show we are succeeding on that mission [to be the world's leading entertainment company]," D'Amaro wrote in a shareholder letter. Total operating income for the company grew 43% year over year to $5 billion, above the expected $4.9 billion, which was the guidance Disney shared last quarter. For the full year, the company reported revenue of $102.3 billion, alongside adjusted earnings per share of $7.02. Both metrics beat the Street's expectations of $101.5 billion in sales and $6.93 in adjusted earnings per share. Disney also announced a 33% increase in its dividend to $2 per share, with $1 paid on Jan. 22, 2027, and the rest paid on July 13, 2027. For 2027, Disney expects segment operating income to grow in the high single digits across Experiences, Entertainment, and Sports. Disney guided for double-digit growth in adjusted earnings per share, assuming "no material deterioration of the global macroeconomic environment." For the first quarter, Disney expects total segment operating income of approximately $5.4 billion. A villain shadow show featuring castle projection and fireworks takes place above the castle on Oct. 16, 2026, in Shanghai, China. (VCG/VCG via Getty Images) VCG via Getty Images Parks and streaming strength drives results Overall revenue from the Disney Experiences segment, which includes US parks and experiences and the expanding Disney Cruise Line portfolio, came in higher than expected at a record $10.1 billion, above the $9.9 billion forecast. The company said an 11% increase in global guests, especially at Walt Disney Disneyland Paris, plus increased capacity at Disney Cruise Line following the launches of the Disney Adventure and Disney Destiny, led to the gain. Domestic parks attendance increased by 11% in the quarter. Customers spent more at Disney parks too. Average spending per customer on admissions, food, and merchandise in US parks rose 4%, more than the expected 3.6% in the US. Internationally, sales at Disneyland Paris offset weakness in Hong Kong and Shanghai parks. Prior to results, Jonathan Kees, senior analyst at Daiwa Capital Markets America, said that looking to 2027, experiences and streaming are Disney's two "most important earnings drivers." Disney's entertainment business revenue showed strength yet again, posting a 17% gain year over year in revenue at $11.9 billion, higher than the nearly $11.5 billion predicted. The company said "Toy Story 5" saw 20 million views on its first five days on Disney+, while August was the highest month ever for Marvel Studios viewing. The company is also evolving its subscription options to allow access across platforms. For example, you can watch Hulu on Disney+, but you will need to subscribe to both. Revenue for Disney's sports segment came in at $4.6 billion, also just above the $4.4 billion predicted, boosted by the NFL transaction earlier this year that makes the NFL a minority stakeholder in ESPN. The company plans to spend more on content in 2027, especially on international content, which CFO Hugh Johnson called a "significant growth driver."
